newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigerian strike seen after US Sierra Leone airlift.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian strike seen after US Sierra Leone airlift.

text.p: The United States evacuated more than 900 foreigners fleeing a coup in Sierra Leone and a senior politician said Nigerian troops planned a military strike on Saturday to restore the ousted civilian government.
Nigeria flew in jeeps, armoured personnel carriers and more troops and there were signs that Ghana and Guinea would join in.
Military and diplomatic sources said rebel commanders had joined the coup leaders and were rejecting any mediation to try to reverse the overthrow of the elected government.
Nigeria cut off communications with rebel leader Foday Sankoh, who appealed on Wednesday from the Abuja hotel where he is held for his men to join forces with the army.
Washington, which is suspending the operation of its embassy in Freetown, said it opposed any use of force to bring back civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
"There is no need. We would oppose any further violence," said State Department spokesman John Dinger.

In Ghana's capital Accra, a cabinet minister said President Jerry Rawlings was in telephone contact with Sierra Leone's new military leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah, trying to persuade him to negotiate a political settlement.
Koromah, who seized power last Sunday, has yet to announce a government. The coup has been condemned at home and abroad.
A squadron of 15 helicopters ferried 330 Americans and 600 people from 40 other countries from a hotel in the capital Freetown to the U.S. helicopter carrier USS Kearsarge lying 12 miles offshore.
A rush of frightened foreigners scrambling to leave before any Nigerian strike pushed the number flown from a heliport in the grounds of the Mammy Yoko Hotel to double what was expected.

The last civilian passenger flown out was a young Lebanese woman in the early stages of labour. Doctors said they expected the baby to be delivered later on Friday night on the Kearsarge, which is expected to dock in Conakry, Guinea in two days.
Ghana said it was consulting with Nigeria and Guinea on the situation and prepared troop transport planes, officially to evacuate Ghanaian nationals living in Sierra Leone.

"Instructions have been given emanating from Nigeria that an invasion is to take place tomorrow morning," said veteran politician John Karefa-Smart, who lost the March 1996 presidential election to Kabbah.
Nigeria leads the ECOMOG regional intervention force sent to Liberia in 1990, which also has some troops in Sierra Leone.

Diplomats said the closure of land, sea and air borders, announced by the Freetown authorities on Thursday night, was to stop the Nigerian buildup. Sierra Leonean sources said it was also an attempt to impede the departure of Westerners to minimise chances of military action.

Military and diplomatic sources said leaders of the rebel Revolutionary United Front (RUF), who had been waging a guerrilla campaign since 1991 but were now allied to the coupmakers, entered the capital two days ago.

"The RUF leaders came out of the bush and entered the town. Now it seems the soldiers have got more than they bargained for because the rebels are now calling the shots," a West African peacekeeping officer said.
A diplomat involved with attempts to strike a deal with Koromah said a veteran politician sent to mediation talks at military headquarters on Thursday night found 50 rebel commanders there.
"They were with the sitting coup leaders, who had their military ranks stripped from their uniforms," the diplomat said, quoting the politician.
"It is a serious problem because the rebels have rejected any mediation. They say they are ready to fight to the end and are prepared for anything," he said.
The coup leaders have shown increasing signs of anxiety as foreign countries accelerate the evacuation of their nationals. Former colonial ruler Britain completed its airlift on Thursday.
